items.title: django-dbos
items.text:
DBOS-backed backend for Django's tasks framework: durable background tasks, cron scheduling and optional Sentry monitoring.

from django.tasks import task

@task
def send_welcome_email(user_id: int):
    ...

result = send_welcome_email.enqueue(user_id)  # durable, survives crashes

If you know Django's tasks API, you already know django-dbos: tasks are declared with @task, enqueued with .enqueue(), and results are standard TaskResult objects. Under the hood, executions are DBOS workflows recorded in a system database, which makes them fault-tolerant: if a worker crashes, tasks resume where they stopped.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Python 3.12+
  • Django 6.0+
  • A DBOS system database: PostgreSQL (recommended) or SQLite

items.title: Installation
items.text:
uv add django-dbos

Add the app and register the backend in your settings:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django_dbos",
]

TASKS = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django_dbos.backends.DBOSBackend",
        "QUEUES": ["default", "emails"],
    },
}

Then run the worker:

python manage.py dbos_worker

That's it — every task enqueued through this backend is now durable. See Configuration for the database setup and the available options.

items.text: MIT

items.title: Configuration
items.text: django-dbos is configured through a single DJANGO_DBOS setting.

items.title: System database
items.text:
DBOS records workflow executions in a system database. By default, django-dbos derives its URL from your default Django connection:

  • PostgreSQL: same server, dedicated database dbos_<dbname> (created automatically on first launch, along with DBOS' tables and migrations).
  • SQLite: a <name>-dbos.sqlite file next to your database. Handy for development and tests, not recommended in production.

Two overrides are available, by order of precedence:

  1. DJANGO_DBOS["SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL"]
  2. the DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL environment variable
DJANGO_DBOS = {
    "SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL": "postgresql+psycopg://user:pass@db.example.com:5432/dbos_myproject",
}

Note

The URL only carries DBOS' system tables. Your application data stays in the Django databases you already have; tasks executed by the worker use Django's ORM as usual.

items.title: Options
items.text: Key Default Description NAME "django" DBOS application name. APPLICATION_VERSION auto Application version recorded with workflow executions. By default DBOS derives it from the workflow source code. SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL derived URL of the DBOS system database (see above). SYSTEM_DB_PREFIX "dbos_" Prefix of the derived system database name. SYSTEM_DB_SCHEMA "dbos" Schema holding DBOS system tables (PostgreSQL). QUEUES {"default": None} Declared queues and their options (see below). AUTO_INIT True Initialize DBOS on app ready (disable to control it yourself). SCHEDULER_POLLING_INTERVAL_SEC 30.0 How often the scheduler thread looks for new schedules.

items.title: Queues
items.text:
Queues process task executions concurrently and are declared under DJANGO_DBOS["QUEUES"]. Queue names used by tasks (through queue_name or TASKS[alias]["QUEUES"]) must be declared here.

DJANGO_DBOS = {
    "QUEUES": {
        "default": None,  # no options
        "emails": {
            "worker_concurrency": 4,   # max concurrent executions per worker
            "global_concurrency": 10,  # max concurrent executions across workers
            "limiter": {"limit": 50, "period": 30},  # rate limit
        },
    },
}

items.title: Launching workers
items.text:
Tasks are executed by the dbos_worker management command:

python manage.py dbos_worker

The worker loads tasks from every installed app's tasks (or dbos_tasks) module, launches DBOS' queue workers and the cron scheduler, and shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM/SIGINT.

Use --no-scheduler to run a worker that does not manage cron schedules (useful when running several workers behind a load balancer and you want a dedicated scheduler).

items.title: Cron scheduling
items.text:
Stack @cron on top of @task to run it on a schedule:

from django.tasks import task
from django_dbos import cron

@cron("*/5 * * * *")  # every 5 minutes
@task
def cleanup_expired_sessions(): ...

The expression uses the standard 5-field crontab syntax. A 6-field form with a leading seconds field is also accepted (DBOS supports sub-minute schedules).

Schedules are managed by DBOS, not by the Django process: the worker registers them in the system database (idempotently, on dbos_worker startup) and DBOS fires them even across restarts and deployments. Scheduled executions go through the task's queue and benefit from the same durability and retries as regular tasks.

Note

Scheduled tasks must not require arguments. django-dbos validates this when the module loads.

Run dbos_worker without --no-scheduler so it registers and fires schedules.

items.title: Timezone
items.text: The crontab is evaluated in Django's default timezone (TIME_ZONE) when USE_TZ is enabled, otherwise in UTC.

items.title: Sentry monitoring
items.text:
Install the extra:

uv add django-dbos[sentry]

Scheduled tasks are then monitored with Sentry cron monitors: the monitor is upserted by Sentry on each check-in, so there is nothing to create in the UI. Its slug is derived from the task name (myapp.tasks.cleanup → myapp-tasks-cleanup).

Options of @cron:

@cron("*/5 * * * *", sentry_monitor_config=None)  # disable monitoring for this task

@cron(
    "0 0 * * *",
    sentry_monitor_config={
        "schedule": {"type": "crontab", "value": "0 0 * * *"},
        "timezone": "Europe/Paris",
        "checkin_margin": 2,  # hours of tolerance
        "max_runtime": 2 * 60 * 60,  # alert if it runs longer
    },
)

By default (no sentry_monitor_config), the monitor configuration is derived from the crontab. Sub-minute schedules cannot be represented as Sentry monitors and are simply not monitored.

Without sentry-sdk installed, everything is a no-op.

items.title: Tasks
items.text:
django-dbos implements Django's tasks framework: tasks are plain module-level functions decorated with @task.

from django.tasks import task

@task
def send_welcome_email(user_id: int) -> None:
    ...

Enqueue it anywhere (views, forms, other tasks...):

result = send_welcome_email.enqueue(user_id)
# or, for async views:
result = await send_welcome_email.aenqueue(user_id)

result is a standard Django TaskResult; with supports_get_result backends you can poll it from anywhere:

result.refresh()
result.status        # TaskResultStatus.READY / RUNNING / SUCCESSFUL / FAILED
result.return_value  # only available when SUCCESSFUL

items.title: Deferred tasks
items.text:
Use .using(run_after=...) to run a task later (an aware datetime or a timedelta):

from datetime import timedelta

send_report.using(run_after=timedelta(hours=1)).enqueue()

items.title: Priorities
items.text:
Django priorities (-100 to 100, higher first) map onto DBOS queue priorities.

@task(priority=50)
def urgent_task(): ...

items.title: Task options
items.text:
DBOS-specific options are attached with @dbos_params:

from django_dbos import dbos_params

@dbos_params(
    step_retries_allowed=True,  # retry the task function on failure
    step_max_attempts=5,
    step_backoff_rate=2.0,
    deduplication_id="nightly-cleanup",  # reject duplicate enqueues
    workflow_timeout=3600,  # seconds
    max_recovery_attempts=10,  # DBOS recovery after worker crashes
)
@task
def cleanup(): ...

Tip

@dbos_params works whether it is above or below @task, and is inert if the task ends up on a non-DBOS backend (handy in tests).

items.title: Options reference
items.text: Option Default Description step_retries_allowed False Retry the task function on failure. step_max_attempts 3 Max attempts when step retries are enabled. step_interval_seconds 1.0 Delay between step retries. step_backoff_rate 2.0 Multiplier applied to the interval after each failure. deduplication_id None While a workflow with this ID is enqueued or running, further enqueues raise an error. queue_partition_key None Partition key for partitioned queues. workflow_timeout None Max wall-clock duration of the whole execution, in seconds. max_recovery_attempts DBOS default Recovery attempts after a worker crash. durable_operations False Enable durable primitives inside the task (see below).

items.title: Durable workflows
items.text:
By default, a task's function runs as a single checkpointed DBOS step: if the worker crashes mid-execution, the task restarts from the beginning. For long-running, multi-stage tasks you can opt into DBOS' durable primitives with durable_operations=True: the function then runs at workflow level and calls get_dbos_context() to checkpoint its work explicitly.

from django_dbos import dbos_params, get_dbos_context

@dbos_params(durable_operations=True)
@task
def onboard_user(user_id: int) -> None:
    ctx = get_dbos_context()

    ctx.run_step(send_welcome_email, user_id)  # checkpointed
    ctx.sleep(86400)  # one day, durably: the worker can crash, it resumes
    ctx.run_step(send_followup_email, user_id)

Available on the context:

Method Description run_step(func, *args, name=...) Execute a function as a checkpointed step. run_step_async(...) Async variant. sleep(seconds) / sleep_async(seconds) Durable sleep: the workflow stops and resumes later. set_event(key, value) Publish an event on the current workflow. get_event(workflow_id, key) Wait for an event from another workflow. send(workflow_id, message, topic) Send a durable message to another workflow. recv(topic, timeout_seconds) Wait for a durable message. start_child_workflow(func, *args) Start a child workflow without waiting for it.

Warning

With durable_operations=True, the task function must be deterministic and is responsible for checkpointing its side effects through steps. Keep the default (single step) unless you need durable sleeps or multi-stage checkpointing.

items.title: Running task functions directly
items.text:
The simplest way to test a task body is to bypass the backend entirely:

from django_dbos.test import run_task, arun_task

def test_send_email():
    result = run_task(send_email, "kevin@example.com")
    assert result == "sent to kevin@example.com"

run_task executes the function synchronously in-process (async task functions are bridged with async_to_sync).

items.title: Using another backend
items.text:
If your tasks must go through the tasks API, point them at Django's immediate or dummy backend in tests:

from django.test import override_settings

@override_settings(TASKS={"default": {"BACKEND": "django.tasks.backends.dummy.DummyBackend"}})
def test_something(): ...

items.title: structlog
items.text:
django-dbos logs through structlog under the django_dbos logger. Use structlog's testing utilities to assert on log output:

from structlog.testing import capture_logs

def test_enqueue_logs(capsys):
    with capture_logs() as logs:
        send_email.enqueue("kevin@example.com")
    assert any(event == "enqueued task" for event in [log["event"] for log in logs])

items.title: Testing scheduled tasks
items.text: @cron only registers the schedule; test the task body itself with run_task. For end-to-end schedule testing, see the integration suite of django-dbos itself (tests/test_integration.py), which runs against a live DBOS system database.
